description: We are developing a high-fidelity, interactive simulation experience that turns complex space agency data into an immersive, choice-driven user journey. Our platform balances strict engineering logic with exceptional design to make complex mission tracking accessible and engaging. We are a fast-moving, multi-disciplinary team looking for final collaborators with passion or expertise in data systems, core web development, graphics, interactive design, and technical project coordination.
summary: RIFT Space Command. Mission Risk is a space mission planner and simulator. It puts the player in the role of a Chief Mission Executive who is responsible for designing a spacecraft by selecting its components and managing the available budget. The player must also choose a launch vehicle and plan an orbit while considering the different risks involved. Mission Risk combines space science and engineering principles with NASA data and simulation techniques to show how technical and financial decisions can affect the outcome of a mission. Players can explore factors such as spacecraft weight and power consumption along with communication with Earth and orbital conditions. They can also study the proximity of other objects in space and understand the risks they may create. The aim of Mission Risk is to make space technology easier to understand by turning complex mission planning concepts into an enjoyable decision making game. It helps players understand how science and engineering are used in space missions and how resources can be managed effectively. It also teaches players what makes a space mission safer and more likely to succeed.
details:
RIFT Space Command – Mission Risk

RIFT stands for Resourceful Intelligence for Flight and Technology. It is an independent student-developed project created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge Space Mission Design Game.

What does our project do and how does it work?

Mission Risk is an interactive 3D space mission planning and simulation game. Players take the role of a mission commander and experience different stages of planning and managing a space mission.

The game takes players through an interactive environment where they attend mission briefings, make decisions with mission teams, manage budgets, select spacecraft equipment and launch vehicles, choose trajectories and proceed towards launch. The experience includes interactive mission areas, a rocket launch sequence, orbital mission scenarios and mission outcome evaluation.

Players must balance their available budget with equipment quality and mission requirements. Their choices influence the calculated mission success rate and final outcome.

The game is supported by a Python-based physics backend that performs scientific calculations and provides simulation results through a REST API.

What problem does it address?

Space mission planning involves complex engineering concepts such as spacecraft design, propulsion, orbital mechanics, atmospheric conditions, communication systems and resource management.

These concepts can be difficult for students and beginners to understand through theoretical learning alone. Mission Risk addresses this gap by bringing several of these concepts together in an interactive environment where users can make decisions and explore their consequences.

What benefits does it provide?

The project introduces users to important space engineering principles through practical decision-making. It encourages logical thinking, problem-solving, scientific curiosity and responsible resource management.

It also demonstrates how different spacecraft systems and mission requirements are connected, helping users understand why engineering decisions must be carefully balanced.

What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to make space science and engineering more accessible and engaging for students and space enthusiasts. We want to encourage more young people to explore aerospace engineering, astronomy, physics and space technology.

Mission Risk can serve as an educational starting point for understanding how space missions are designed, simulated and evaluated.

What technologies and tools did we use?

1. Game Engine and Frontend

  • Godot Engine 4.x – 3D game development and interactive environments.
  • GDScript – Gameplay logic, player interactions, mission progression and UI.

2. Backend and Programming Languages

  • Python 3.12+ – Scientific calculations and simulation logic.
  • FastAPI – Backend framework for building REST APIs.
  • Uvicorn – ASGI server for running the backend.
  • Pydantic – Data validation and API request handling.

3. Scientific and Mathematical Libraries

  • NumPy – Numerical computing and array operations.
  • SciPy – Scientific computing, numerical integration and optimization.
  • SGP4 and Skyfield – Orbital computation libraries included in the dependency lockfile.
  • SymPy – Symbolic mathematics library included in the dependency lockfile.
  • Astropy – Astronomy library included in the dependency lockfile.
  • Numba – Numerical performance library included in the dependency lockfile.
  • Pint – Physical units library included in the dependency lockfile.

4. Data and Communication

  • JSON – Mission configuration, spacecraft catalogues and narrative data.
  • HTTP REST API – Communication between the Godot frontend and Python backend.
  • Godot HTTPRequest – Sending and receiving simulation data.

5. Testing and Development

  • Pytest – Backend testing.
  • HTTPX – HTTP client and API testing.
  • Git and GitHub – Source code management and project hosting.

How is our project creative and innovative?

The main creative aspect of RIFT is the combination of interactive first-person 3D gameplay with a separate scientific physics simulation backend.

Instead of presenting mission planning as a collection of facts or questions, we allow players to experience a mission environment, interact with different teams, make engineering decisions and observe their effects on the mission.

The integration of gameplay with calculations involving orbital mechanics, rocket ascent, atmospheric modelling, communication link budgets and propulsion uncertainty gives the project both an educational and technical dimension.

What factors did our team consider?

During development, we considered mission budgets, spacecraft equipment selection, payload requirements, launch vehicle capabilities, propulsion, trajectory planning, atmospheric conditions, orbital mechanics and communication requirements.

We also considered the relationship between technical decisions and mission outcomes, the usability of the game environment and the need to make complex scientific concepts understandable to beginners.

Our goal was to create an educational experience that combines space science, engineering concepts and interactive decision-making in one platform.
